A geometry-first approach to fundamental physics

Can the structure of nature emerge from geometry?
From geometry to observables.

Born–Hopf Geometry asks whether compact geometry, a finite reciprocal carrier and its native operators can determine the structure of quantum states, particles, interactions and cosmology. Its latest papers develop more explicit transition comparisons and source operators, while keeping the passage to measured rates and couplings an explicit scientific test.

The working idea

Geometry as a source of constraints.

Not a metaphor for physics, but an attempt to make physics follow from operators that geometry allows.

01

A compact starting point

The three-sphere S³ is not an ordinary ball in space. It is a compact three-dimensional geometry, closely related to rotations and unit quaternions. Its symmetries provide a structured starting point rather than an unbounded continuum of arbitrary choices.

Explore →02

Position and momentum together

The framework studies a reciprocal eight-dimensional geometry M₈ built from paired position-like and momentum-like sectors. Their relations, phases and operators are used to formulate physical kinematics.

Explore →03

Observable consequences

Finite geometry is only the beginning. A particle mass, decay width or gravitational coupling must follow from an action, a realized source and a map to a measurable quantity—not merely from a suggestive number.

The central question

A theory of physics should do more than describe the patterns we already know. Ideally, it should explain why those patterns are possible in the first place. Born–Hopf Geometry asks whether the mathematical structure of a compact geometric system can sharply restrict what a physical world can contain—and eventually determine measurable outcomes.

This reverses a familiar order of construction. Rather than beginning with an inventory of particles, forces and fitted interaction parameters, the programme begins with distinguishable geometric relations and investigates which states, interactions and responses follow from them. Existing physics is an indispensable benchmark, but copying its familiar mechanisms is not the objective.

Why the geometry matters

A three-sphere has rich geometry without boundaries. It can also be described through the group of unit quaternions, SU(2), which makes its symmetries concrete and calculable. The Hopf fibration organizes it into interlinked circles over a two-sphere. Finite exceptional patterns—such as those related to the 24-cell and 600-cell—provide additional, highly constrained geometric structures.

None of this means that a particle is literally a vertex of a polytope. The research task is to construct the relevant operators and show why their behavior corresponds to an actual particle, interaction or measurement. Explore the mathematical geometry or read Paper I-A and Paper I-B.

A research programme, not a shortcut

The series develops its argument in stages: geometric constitution and finite momentum, reciprocal kinematics, dynamics and spectral responses, finite quantum mechanics, matter and interaction carriers, gravity and cosmology, and strong-interaction structures. Each stage inherits conditions from earlier ones. Those conditions matter: a mathematically available operator is not automatically an experimentally observed phenomenon.

For the full explanation, start with the guided framework. For the specific questions the framework must answer, see From geometry to observables. The 31 versioned manuscripts and proof-chain archive supply the technical record.

Observable-first research

An explanation should reach a measurement.

A geometric analogy is not a physical prediction. The research program treats source occurrence, dynamical evolution, a detector-facing readout and independent comparison as separate obligations. The papers and proof-chain records are available so that each step can be examined.
